key_insight: Neural scaling laws meaningfully describe how performance of weather-emulation models improves with model size, data, and compute, and continual training (streaming updates) enables more predictable, sample-efficient scaling in an operational forecasting setting.
problem_solved: Provides an empirical framework for understanding and optimizing how model size, dataset scale, and training strategy (especially continual updates) interact for weather-forecasting models, addressing design uncertainty for scientific ML deployments.
method: Use a minimal, scalable Swin Transformer architecture as a general-purpose backbone for weather emulation.
Run systematic scaling experiments varying model size, dataset size, and compute to measure performance trends.
Apply continual training (streaming/incremental updates) to simulate operational non-stationary data and evaluate its effect on scaling and sample efficiency.
impact: Gives practitioners actionable guidance to choose model/data/compute trade-offs and adopt continual-training workflows for robust, efficient weather emulation—accelerating the path toward foundation models in scientific domains.
visual_elements: Scaling curves: performance metric (e.g., forecast error) vs. model parameters / dataset size / compute with fitted scaling-law lines
Schematic of the minimal Swin Transformer backbone highlighting patching, self-attention windows, and parameter scaling
Flow diagram of continual-training pipeline: streaming observations → incremental updates → evaluation on shifting test windows
Geographical forecast heatmaps or error-difference maps showing qualitative improvements as scale or continual training increases
paper_title: On Neural Scaling Laws for Weather Emulation through Continual Training
paper_authors: Shashank Subramanian, Alexander Kiefer, Arnur Nigmetov, Amir Gholami, Dmitriy Morozov
